world_behind.title: A handoff already under way
world_behind.text: The chapter begins mid-institution. Nephi is still alive in verse 1, dead by verse 12, and the record changes hands in between. Ancient records rarely narrate their own transfer; this one spends its first eight verses on the terms of the transfer before telling the reader that the previous keeper died.

world_behind.title: Two sets of plates, still running in parallel
world_behind.text: Verse 3 has Nephi assigning the history to "his other plates" and this record to Jacob. That division was announced back in 1 Nephi 9, and this is the first time the reader sees it enforced on a new keeper. The large plates continue under the kings; the small plates go to a priest.

world_behind.title: Throne names
world_behind.text: Verse 11 has successors called "second Nephi, third Nephi," whatever their birth names. Egyptian and Mesopotamian kingship both used regnal names distinct from personal ones, and Israel's own kings sometimes took new names at accession. What the verse describes is a colony inventing dynastic nomenclature within one generation of arrival.

world_behind.title: A priesthood without Levites
world_behind.text: Verse 18 says Jacob and Joseph were consecrated priests and teachers "by the hand of Nephi." Nobody in this colony is of Levi. The consecration language is Aaronic; the verb is the one used of Aaron's sons in Numbers 3. But the hand doing the consecrating is a brother's, and the record does not pause to justify it.

world_behind.title: The watchman's rule
world_behind.text: Verse 19 works from Ezekiel (Ezek. 33:6): warn, or the blood of the unwarned is required at your hand. Ezekiel says "hand"; Jacob says "garments." The shift from hand to garment moves the stain from the act to the person, and garments in this record are already the standing figure for a state one is found in at judgment.

world_behind.title: The seven names
world_behind.text: Verse 13's list (Nephites, Jacobites, Josephites, Zoramites, Lamanites, Lemuelites, Ishmaelites) is a lineage register, and the founders are the seven men who left Jerusalem or married into the party. The colony has become tribes in two generations.

world_behind.title: Wives, concubines, gold
world_behind.text: Verses 15 and 16 name the two offenses in the order Deuteronomy 17 forbids them to a king: multiplying wives, and multiplying silver and gold. The people are copying a monarchy, and the chapter reports it in the sentence right after it finishes describing how their monarchy was set up.

words.text: The instruction is to touch the history "save it were lightly," and the adverb is doing editorial work. It does not forbid history; it rations it. Everything narrative in this book from here forward is there under a quota, which is worth remembering whenever the record seems to skip decades in a clause.

The one occurrence in the whole record. It comes from Psalm 95, where Israel provoked God at Meribah and was sworn out of his rest, and the psalm is the passage Hebrews later builds its rest argument on. Jacob imports the technical term intact. The wilderness generation is being offered to this colony as its own likeliest future.

To anoint is to pour oil on a man, the act that made a king a king in Israel, and Messiah is the word for one who has had it done to him. Nephi performs it for his successor. No other anointing of a Nephite king is reported anywhere in the record; the royal anointings that follow are Jaredite, in Ether, and Benjamin later consecrates Mosiah rather than anointing him (Mosiah 6:3). The colony uses the old ceremony once, at the founding of its monarchy.

The adverb hedges twice running. The people "indulge themselves somewhat in wicked practices" (v. 15), and they are "lifted up somewhat in pride" (v. 16). Jacob is reporting a beginning rather than a settled condition, and the measured word is his own. It does not last. The temple sermon this chapter is introducing calls the same conduct abominable and a grosser crime (Jacob 2:22), with no adverb attached.

cites.quote: indulge themselves somewhat in wicked practices

spans.text: indulge themselves somewhat in wicked practices

words.text: Also unique here in this record. In the King James Bible an errand is always a commission to carry a message. Abraham's servant will not eat until he has told his errand, and Ehud has a secret errand for the king. Jacob does not say he prepared a sermon; he says he obtained an errand, so the temple speech that follows is a delivery.

To enlarge, and in the King James usage to make great by treating as great. Jacob and his brother magnify an office rather than a name. The word appears twice in this record and both times in Jacob's mouth, and both times what is enlarged is a duty.

phrases.term: A few of the things which I considered to be most precious
phrases.text: The selection rule for everything that follows, and it is personal. Not what happened, not what mattered to the nation, but what one man appraised as most precious. The record is candid that its contents passed through a single judgment, and the phrase invites the reader to notice whose.

phrases.term: Engraven the heads of them upon these plates
phrases.text: What is asked for is a heading. Jacob is told to record the topic sentences of sacred preaching and touch on them as far as the metal allows. It is the closest the record comes to describing its own compression, and it explains why sermons here often read like summaries with one verse of full quotation inside them.

phrases.term: For Christ's sake, and for the sake of our people
phrases.text: Two beneficiaries, in that order, for a writing project. The phrase occurs in only one other place in this record. Everything Jacob selects has to pass a test with two names on it, and the second name is the reason the first is not left abstract.

phrases.term: Lest by any means he should swear in his wrath they should not enter in
phrases.text: The oath is the point. God's refusal in Psalm 95 is a sworn act, and that is why the psalm and Hebrews both treat exclusion from rest as legally settled. The only other place this record swears that oath is Alma 12, where the same psalm is worked through at length.

phrases.term: Having wielded the sword of Laban in their defence
phrases.text: The sword's fourth appearance and its plainest. Taken in a dark street, carried across an ocean, used as a pattern for an armory, and here simply wielded by the man who took it, for the people it was taken for. The verse is a eulogy, and this is the line it chooses.

phrases.term: Let them be of whatever name they would
phrases.text: The concession clause is the interesting part. The people are said to have imposed the throne name regardless of the man's own name, and the sentence shrugs at the man. A memorial practice invented out of love for one king becomes, in one clause, a thing done to his successors.

phrases.term: Such as like unto David of old desiring many wives and concubines
phrases.text: The record's first criticism of David, and it arrives as a description of what the people were imitating. Jacob will make the argument in the next chapter. Here the name functions as a diagnosis: the problem is prestige, and the prestige is scriptural.

phrases.term: Answering the sins of the people upon our own heads
phrases.text: Not sharing the guilt, but answering for it. The construction makes the teacher a defendant at the people's trial, liable for what he did not do rather than for what he did. It is the strongest statement of ministerial risk in the record, and it is made by a man describing why he is about to give a hard sermon.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: An editorial brief quoted whole
verses.text: The record sets out the instructions the new writer received, keeping their wording: write "a few of the things which I considered to be most precious," do "not touch, save it were lightly, concerning the history of this people," and where there is preaching or revelation or prophecy, "engraven the heads of them upon these plates." Three rules, one positive and two restrictive. Verse 1 dates the handover at fifty-five years from Lehi's departure, which is the second of seven such totals in these books after 2 Nephi 5:28. A book that changes hands here explains its own selection policy before writing a line of content.

verses.label: v. 7
verses.title: A warning borrowed in the New Testament's wording
verses.text: The record reaches for an Israelite precedent and takes it in a specific form: "lest by any means he should swear in his wrath they should not enter in, as in the provocation in the days of temptation while the children of Israel were in the wilderness." The underlying text is Psalm 95:8–11, but "the provocation" and "the day of temptation in the wilderness" are the phrases of Hebrews 3:8–11, not the Psalm's own. The record pairs the borrowed clause with its own recurring word, "enter into his rest," which appears three times in this chapter and the next.

verses.label: v. 12
verses.title: Five words for the death of the protagonist
verses.text: The record gives the whole notice as "And it came to pass that Nephi died." Two verses have just been spent on why the people loved him, listing his protection, the sword of Laban, and his labor. The eulogy precedes the death and is four times its length. Nothing follows about burial, mourning, or succession beyond the naming rule already given, and the next verse moves straight to terminology.

verses.label: v. 13–14
verses.title: A list of seven names given in order to be abandoned
verses.text: The record names the divisions, Nephites, Jacobites, Josephites, Zoramites, Lamanites, Lemuelites, Ishmaelites, and then states a policy in the first person: "I, Jacob, shall not hereafter distinguish them by these names." The replacement is a two-part functional test, those who "seek to destroy the people of Nephi" against "those who are friendly to Nephi." The same seven names appear again at 4 Nephi 1:37–38 and at Mormon 1:8, each time immediately before a similar collapse into two.

verses.label: v. 15
verses.title: The fault named by citing scripture as its precedent
verses.text: The record declines to describe the practice in general terms and supplies a source: the people began "desiring many wives and concubines," specified as "like unto David of old" and "also Solomon, his son." The charge is that they are imitating figures their own records honor, which is why Jacob 2:23–24 has to argue the point at length and quote a divine judgment on those two kings by name. A fault introduced here as an allusion becomes a doctrinal argument one chapter later.

verses.label: v. 17–19
verses.title: An office defined by what it costs to hold
verses.text: The record states the terms in the language of liability: the priests take "the responsibility, answering the sins of the people upon our own heads if we did not teach them the word of God with all diligence," so that "their blood might not come upon our garments." The clause is stated twice over, positively and then negatively, inside verse 19. Verse 17 also records a procedural step before the sermon, "having first obtained mine errand from the Lord," which fixes the sequence: authorization first, teaching second, and personal exposure as the standing condition of both.

chapter.title: A book that begins with its own terms of service
chapter.text: Before any sermon, prophecy, or allegory, the reader is told what this record is allowed to contain and who decided. Jacob 1 is a record-keeper's preface turned into a chapter, and it makes the rest of the book legible: when Jacob says he lacks room, the reader already knows the constraint is inherited.

chapter.title: The founder's death gets four words
chapter.text: Nephi's dying is surrounded by his anointing of a king, the people's love for him, and the naming convention built in his honor. The death itself is a single short sentence. The chapter grieves by arrangement, a very different instinct from the psalm in 2 Nephi 4.

chapter.title: Decline arrives immediately
chapter.text: There is no golden age between verse 12 and verse 15. The second king's reign is where wives, concubines, gold, and pride enter. The record's long pattern of prosperity turning to pride is usually introduced later; here it is running before the founder is cold.

chapter.title: The naming problem is solved by hostility
chapter.text: Verse 14 defines Nephite and Lamanite by disposition toward the people of Nephi rather than by descent from Nephi or Laman. Every later use of those two words in this record carries that definition, including the passages where the categories change hands entirely.

chapter.title: Priesthood is simply asserted
chapter.text: The chapter reports consecration by Nephi's hand without addressing lineage, and no part of the record ever returns to defend it. This book is unusually careful about legal form: witnesses, oaths, records. It is silent exactly where a Levitical objection would land.

chapter.title: The teacher is placed at risk
chapter.text: The final verse makes the accountability run upward from the people to the teacher rather than downward. Jacob is not describing a privilege of office; he is describing a liability, and he is describing it immediately before spending two chapters saying things his congregation will not enjoy.

chapter.title: The chapter is the hinge between two kinds of book
chapter.text: The chapter carries the handover in nineteen verses and states the rules before applying them: write "a few of the things which I considered to be most precious," do "not touch, save it were lightly, concerning the history," and "engraven the heads of them" of preaching, revelation, and prophecy. What follows in Jacob 2 through 6 is one sermon, one long allegory, and one summary chapter, with the history reduced to the naming convention at verses 9 through 14 and the single line at verse 12, "And it came to pass that Nephi died."

applications.title: Name your selection rule
applications.text: Jacob wrote down what he judged most precious and said so. In whatever you record, whether a journal, a family history, or notes from a meeting, try stating the rule you are selecting by. It makes the omissions honest.

applications.title: Write down the topic sentences
applications.text: When you cannot capture everything, capture the headings. Jacob's constraint is a practical method for anyone with more experience than time to record it.

applications.title: Watch the second reign
applications.text: The chapter's warning is about how quickly an inheritance is spent. Look at something you received already built: a ward, a business, a family culture. Ask what has drifted in it during your own tenure.

applications.title: Check what you are imitating
applications.text: The people were not inventing; they were copying a prestigious model. Identify one practice you have adopted mainly because respected people do it, and evaluate it on its own terms.

applications.title: Obtain the errand first
applications.text: Before giving counsel you expect to be unwelcome, do what verse 17 puts first in the sentence. The order in the verse is commission, then teaching.

applications.title: Take the responsibility
applications.text: Jacob magnified an office by enlarging its duty. In any assignment you hold, name the one duty you have been treating as optional, and treat it as the office itself.

questions.text: What do I consider most precious, and would anyone reading what I actually record be able to tell?
What is my version of the provocation, the pattern I keep repeating that would keep me out of rest?
Whose name am I trying to keep in remembrance, and is honoring it the same as obeying it?
Do I sort people by what they are descended from or by how they behave toward what I love?
When did I last teach or counsel someone without first asking whether I had an errand to?
Whose blood, in Jacob's sense, might be on my garments? Who have I not warned because it would be uncomfortable?
